# srelens

> srelens is a Kubernetes workspace — available as a native desktop GUI app and a fast standalone Terminal UI written in Rust (`srectl`, formerly srelens-tui) for browsing, inspecting, and operating Kubernetes clusters. It is built with a Rust core (kube-rs), features an in-memory Informer cache, deep Helm inspection, and includes a built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) server and embedded AI assistant that exposes supported backend capabilities as AI-callable tools.

Key facts:
- Product type: desktop application (Kubernetes IDE / cluster workspace) & standalone Terminal UI (srectl)
- Platforms: macOS, Windows, Linux (Tauri v2 desktop app; standalone binary CLI / TUI)
- Status: available — desktop installers on GitHub Releases for macOS (Apple Silicon + Intel), Windows (x64), and Linux (x86_64); srectl CLI archives for macOS (Apple Silicon + Intel), Windows (x64), and Linux (x86_64 + aarch64, glibc and static musl); srectl also installable via Homebrew (`brew install srelens/tap/srectl`)
- Price: free, open source under the MIT license
- Architecture: Rust core using kube-rs to talk to the Kubernetes API directly — no Electron, no Node.js in the core app runtime
- Lineage: inspired by Lens / Freelens (Electron-based Kubernetes IDEs); srelens is a clean-room rebuild of that workflow, not a fork. Not affiliated with Mirantis (Lens) or the Freelens project.
- Desktop screenshots in both app themes and srectl text captures, all from a live kind cluster.

## Features

- Standalone pure-Rust Terminal UI (`srectl`): in-memory Informer cache (instant screen switching for views already opened), Tab-completed command bar (`:po`, `:svc`, `:deploy`, `:helm`, `:workloads`, `:topology`, `:gpuinfo`, `:top`, `:ctx`), deep Helm inspector & values diff, interactive themes, and embedded AI assistant
- Multi-cluster management: every context in your local kubeconfig, cluster hotbar, multiple kubeconfig files, context profiles and custom ordering
- Resource browser covering 35 built-in Kubernetes kinds plus any CRD: workloads (Pods, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs), config and storage (ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, PVs, StorageClasses), networking (Services, Ingresses, NetworkPolicies, EndpointSlices), RBAC (Roles, ClusterRoles, bindings, ServiceAccounts), admission webhooks, autoscaling, Namespaces, Nodes, Events
- Live streaming resource watches (kube-rs watch streams, not polling)
- Browser-style tabs: each tab is a (cluster, resource-kind) view
- Schema-aware YAML editor with autocomplete and linting driven by the cluster's OpenAPI schema; create resources from templates and apply
- In-pod interactive terminals (exec), opened as tabs in the app
- Pod and workload log streaming with container filtering and search
- Port forwarding: start/stop/monitor forwards with a status indicator
- Helm release inspection
- Custom resource (CRD) browsing grouped by API group
- Command palette (Cmd/Ctrl-K): global resource search with deep links
- Cluster metrics: CPU/memory for nodes and pods via metrics-server
- Node and workload operations: scale, rollout restart, evict pod, cordon node, drain node — all destructive actions are confirmation-gated
- Toolbox: manage kubectl, krew, and helm CLI installations from inside the app

## AI / MCP integration

Supported backend capabilities are registered in a shared capability registry and exposed through the built-in MCP server. Agents such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, or other MCP-capable clients connect over stdio (by spawning `srelens --mcp-stdio` via the installed CLI) or loopback HTTP (default `http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp`). The MCP settings panel generates ready-to-paste client config. Mutating tools require an explicit `_confirm: true` argument before they run. Cluster credentials never leave the machine: srelens connects directly to API servers using the local kubeconfig.

## Common questions

- Does srelens replace kubectl? No — it complements it. srelens talks to the Kubernetes API directly through kube-rs and doesn't need kubectl for that; srectl uses your local kubectl for pod and node shells and your local helm for rollbacks. It is a workspace for investigation and operations, not a scripting/automation tool.
- Is it free? Yes, free and MIT-licensed.
- Where does cluster data go? Nowhere — the app runs locally and talks directly to your clusters.

## Demo environment used for screenshots

kind cluster `srelens-demo` (context `kind-srelens-demo`): 1 control-plane + 2 worker nodes, Kubernetes v1.36.1; namespaces `payments`, `checkout`, `monitoring`. Workloads: a `payments-api` Deployment (2 replicas, nginx:1.27-alpine), a `redis` StatefulSet, a deliberately crash-looping `ledger-worker` Deployment (it logs `connecting to ledger-db:5432`, then `fatal: connection refused`, and exits 1) in `payments`; a `checkout-web` Deployment and a `cart-sync` CronJob in `checkout`; a `status-exporter` Deployment in `monitoring`. The feature captures add a Helm release `podinfo` in `checkout` with two revisions (revision 2 raises replicas from 1 to 2), Argo CD with a `guestbook` Application, and MetalLB in BGP mode peering with an FRR router container, with a `payments-api-lb` LoadBalancer Service in `payments`. metrics-server installed for live usage numbers. For the srectl GPU view only, a simulated NVIDIA A100 GPU node was added with kwok (no GPU exists) and removed afterwards. The srectl screens are text captures of v0.16.0 against the same cluster, shown on https://srelens.com/tui/ and https://srelens.com/docs/tui/.
